paragraphs.source_en: It was on the ninth day of the first month in the tenth year of Keichō that Ieyasu finally resolved to leave Edo for the capital and attend the emperor. By then, Hidetada and his close retainers had already made meticulous arrangements. Evidently, the counsel of Tōdō Takatora and Tenkai had made little difference.

paragraphs.source_en: On his journey to the capital, Ieyasu paused briefly at Hakone to bathe in the hot springs, then reached Sunpu Castle. He intended to rest there for a time, observe public opinion and the temper of the people, and afterward proceed to Fushimi Castle; the date was set for the nineteenth day of the second month. Only then would word be sent to Hidetada in Edo, whereupon Hidetada would depart with the force that stood fully prepared.

paragraphs.source_en: Ieyasu was astonished by these rumors. He had always known that governing was no easy task, but he had never imagined that, through the ignorance of the people, his goodwill might become the seed of ambitions and disaster. He concluded that Hidetada’s force must be reorganized. If it numbered only three or five thousand, people might indeed draw the wrong conclusion and cause a disturbance that ought never to occur.

paragraphs.source_en: Ieyasu’s own procession remained exceedingly modest, inferior even to that of a minor lord with a domain of ten thousand koku. But Hidetada, who was to become the next shogun, must, just as Tenkai had said, strike terror at a glance and extinguish all thoughts of rebellion. And so, from Hikone, Ieyasu dispatched an urgent messenger to race back to Edo and command Hidetada to prepare with the utmost care.
